newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: DEVELOPMENT BANK MAPS OUT FINANCIAL FUTURE.
newsitem.headline: DEVELOPMENT BANK MAPS OUT FINANCIAL FUTURE.

text.p: More market-related interest rates and greater efficiencies will ensure the long-term viability of the Development Bank of Southern Africa but it would need interim measures to support it for the next three years, chief executive Ian Goldin said on Tuesday.
He briefed South Africa's parliamentary finance committee on a bill aimed at reconstituting and incorporating the bank in terms of the companies act as a development finance institution.
Goldin said the bill would provide the bank with a share capital of five billion rand, of which two billion rand would be held by government.
This would help the bank retain its Triple A rating in the face of the withdrawal of government guarantees and allow it to continue to provide low interest loans to high risk infrastructure projects.
Goldin said the bill had become necessary because of the change in the constitution and the bank's conversion from a funder of South Africa's former black homelands into a development institution.
"We exist to take risks that the private sector is not prepared to take in infrastructure investments," he said.

Golding said its Triple A rating was also important because the bank had not received any government funding since 1994 and about 75 percent of its funding came from the financial markets. It borrowed about one billion rand a year from the market.
The balance of its funding came mainly from concessionary, bilateral sources and, to a lesser extent, from the repayment of apartheid era loans by the government.
Goldin said the bank expected to boost its revenue from loans from its recent increase in interest rates from nine percent to 14 percent.
"We are moving closer to the market but we exist as a concessionary lender, to take risks that the private sector won't take," he said.
The increase in interest rates would only kick in in two or three years' time because of the time it took to disburse funds to projects.
"As a result of this we are particularly concerned about the next three years. We believe that from three years time we will be viable as a result of the new financial policies."

He was holding discussions with Finance Minister Trevor Manuel about "some interim measures for the next three years" so that it could sustain the massive increase in lending expected for infrastructural projects.
This would probably be provided through the re-negotiation of repayment terms for loans granted before 1994.

He did not envisage outside shareholders taking control of the bank, although regional governments and bilateral agencies such as the Commonwealth Development Corporation could eventually take up shares.
The bank's loan book currently stands at about 12 billion rand and Goldin said it was growing rapidly.

He said that the bank was engaged in "very preliminary" discussions with the World Bank as well as other agencies such as the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, African Development Bank and the European Investment Bank for both technica assistance and grants.
